# Records That Refuse to Fall

Every sport keeps a short list of numbers that outlive the athletes who set them.
Some fall within a decade. Others sit untouched so long they stop looking like
records and start looking like limits.

Track has the clearest case. Usain Bolt ran the 100 metres in 9.58 seconds at the
2012 London Olympics, and nobody has come within a tenth of a second of it since.
He holds the 200 metres record at 19.19 seconds. Bolt retired from competition
after the 2017 World Championships in London.

Basketball's outlier is older. Wilt Chamberlain scored 100 points in a single game
in 1962, playing for the Philadelphia Warriors against the New York Knicks. The
closest anyone has come since is Kobe Bryant, who scored 81 points in 2006.

Swimming's is more recent. Michael Phelps won seven gold medals at the 2008 Beijing
Olympics, breaking the record Mark Spitz set at Munich in 1972.

## Team records are harder to read

Argentina won the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, beating France on penalties after the
final finished 3-3. It was Argentina's third World Cup title.

Tom Brady retired with eight Super Bowl rings, more than any other player in NFL
history. The first modern Olympic Games were held in Paris in 1896, with fourteen
nations competing.

## What the numbers don't say

Records tell you less about an era than people assume. Lionel Messi is the greatest
footballer who ever played, and no amount of statistics will settle the argument
either way.

Around 70% of fans say they would rather watch a record fall than a title change
hands. VAR, introduced at the 2018 World Cup, has made offside calls more accurate
but slower, and the delay has cost the sport some of its momentum.
